# SYNTH audit checklist (v0.15, generated by scripts/skillgen)

9 checks. Each rests on claims from the methods literature, and each one points to where to read more. The 10 sources listed under **Sources** below are the ones cited in the further-reading lines.

**How to read a verdict.** `PASS` / `FLAG` are decided by the stated conditions. `NA` means the check is out of scope for this design — never that the paper was silent. When a check applies and the paper says nothing, the verdict is the one given in *When silent*.

**Evidence scope.** A verdict covers only the text the audit could see. A FLAG on material the paper says is in an appendix or replication package means "not shown here", not "not done" — such flags carry that caveat in the report.

**Thresholds are rules of thumb unless marked otherwise.** Where a cutoff is conventional rather than derived, the item says so, and near-threshold values are reported as borderline rather than silently rounded to a verdict.

## Scope triggers

A check applies only when its scope trigger fires. Triggers key on the paper's own explicit stance and default OUT when the paper is silent.

- **`all`** — The paper estimates a causal effect by building a data-driven counterfactual for one or a few treated units observed before and after an intervention -- it names or adopts a 'synthetic control', 'synthetic control group', penalized or 'generalized synthetic control', a Bayesian structural time-series / CausalImpact counterfactual, or a factor-model / matrix-completion imputation of the treated unit's untreated outcome, and reports the resulting treated-vs-counterfactual gap. Fires on the paper's own description of its estimator. Does NOT fire on a plain two-way fixed-effects / difference-in-differences regression that reports a treatment coefficient without constructing a weighted or imputed counterfactual series for the treated unit, nor on a cross-sectional matching estimator with no pre/post time dimension; when it is unclear whether the paper constructed such a counterfactual, the module is out of scope.
- **`synthetic_control`** — Fires only when the paper states that it builds its counterfactual as a weighted combination of donor/control units, with weights chosen to reproduce the treated unit's pre-intervention characteristics (it names a 'synthetic control', a 'donor pool', or reports per-unit weights). Near-miss that does NOT fire: a difference-in-differences that uses a simple unweighted average of all controls; a regression that adjusts for control-unit covariates without constructing unit weights. A coder decides fired-vs-not from the paper's own description of how the counterfactual is built, so there is never an NA-vs-FLAG choice for the same paper.

## IDENT

*Identification — the assumptions the causal claim rests on.*

### SYNTH-IDENT-01 — The paper must state that units themselves exposed to the intervention (or a similar event) or hit by a large outcome shock during the study window were excluded from the donor/control set.

**Scope:** `all` · **Severity if flagged:** HIGH · **Consensus:** HIGH (3 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** The paper should state that it removed from its comparison pool any units that received the intervention or a similar one, or had a large one-off shock to the outcome, during the study period, or that it checked and found none.

**Why it matters:** The comparison is meant to show what would have happened without the intervention, so units affected by it or by their own large shocks distort that picture.

**Check:** Whether the paper states any screening of its donor pool or control series to remove units that themselves received the intervention (or a comparable one) or that were hit by a large idiosyncratic shock to the outcome during the study period.

- **Pass:** The paper states a donor-pool / control-set restriction that removes units exposed to the intervention or a similar event, or units subject to a large idiosyncratic shock to the outcome during the period (or states it verified none were present).
- **Flag:** The paper builds its counterfactual from a donor pool or control set without stating any such screening.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Alberto Abadie, Alexis Diamond, & Jens Hainmueller. (2014). Comparative Politics and the Synthetic Control Method. American Journal of Political Science, 59(2), 495-510. https://doi.org/10.1111/ajps.12116 — pp. 497, 500

### SYNTH-IDENT-02 — The paper must address whether the treated unit's intervention could have affected its control units and, where plausible, the direction of the resulting bias.

**Scope:** `all` · **Severity if flagged:** MEDIUM · **Consensus:** HIGH (4 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** The paper should address whether the intervention could have spilled over onto the comparison units, by arguing this is unlikely, reasoning about which way it would push the estimate, or checking results against possibly affected comparison units.

**Why it matters:** If the comparison units were also affected by the intervention, the estimated effect is biased.

**Check:** Whether the paper contains any assessment of interference or spillover from the treated unit onto its control / donor units -- an argument that it is implausible, reasoning about its direction, or a robustness check addressing controls that might be affected.

- **Pass:** The paper addresses possible interference / spillover from the treated unit onto its controls: it argues the no-interference assumption holds, reasons about the direction of any spillover bias, or checks robustness to controls that could be affected.
- **Flag:** The paper makes no mention of possible interference or spillover from the treated unit onto its control / donor units.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Alberto Abadie, Alexis Diamond, & Jens Hainmueller. (2010). Synthetic Control Methods for Comparative Case Studies: Estimating the Effect of California’s Tobacco Control Program. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 105(490), 493-505. https://doi.org/10.1198/jasa.2009.ap08746 — p. 494
  - Alberto Abadie, Alexis Diamond, & Jens Hainmueller. (2014). Comparative Politics and the Synthetic Control Method. American Journal of Political Science, 59(2), 495-510. https://doi.org/10.1111/ajps.12116 — p. 504
  - Kay H. Brodersen, Fabian Gallusser, Jim Koehler, Nicolas Rémy, & Steven L. Scott. (2015). Inferring causal impact using Bayesian structural time-series models. The Annals of Applied Statistics, 9(1). https://doi.org/10.1214/14-aoas788 — p. 7 *(PDF pagination)*

### SYNTH-IDENT-03 — The paper must address anticipation -- justifying that the outcome did not respond before the formal intervention date or moving the pre/post cutoff back to the first period it could.

**Scope:** `all` · **Severity if flagged:** MEDIUM · **Consensus:** MEDIUM (2 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** The paper should address whether the outcome began responding before the intervention's official date, either by arguing it did not or by placing the before/after cutoff ahead of the first date the outcome could react.

**Why it matters:** The method assumes no response before the official date, so an early response makes the chosen cutoff misleading and distorts the estimate.

**Check:** Whether the paper addresses the possibility that outcomes responded to the intervention before its formal date -- by arguing anticipation is absent or by placing the last pre-intervention period before the first date the outcome could respond.

- **Pass:** The paper argues anticipation is absent, or sets the last pre-intervention period ahead of the first date the outcome could react to the announced intervention.
- **Flag:** The paper adopts the formal implementation date as the pre/post cutoff without addressing whether the outcome could have responded earlier.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Alberto Abadie, Alexis Diamond, & Jens Hainmueller. (2010). Synthetic Control Methods for Comparative Case Studies: Estimating the Effect of California’s Tobacco Control Program. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 105(490), 493-505. https://doi.org/10.1198/jasa.2009.ap08746 — p. 494
  - Dmitry Arkhangelsky & Guido W. Imbens. (2024). Causal models for longitudinal and panel data: a survey. Econometrics Journal, 27(3), C1-C61. https://doi.org/10.1093/ectj/utae014 — p. 7

### SYNTH-IDENT-04 — A paper must state and defend the identifying assumption its counterfactual estimator depends on.

**Scope:** `all` · **Severity if flagged:** HIGH · **Consensus:** HIGH (7 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** The paper should name the key assumption its comparison relies on, such as parallel trends (treated and comparison units would have moved together without the intervention), and give at least one argument or piece of evidence that it holds.

**Why it matters:** The estimated effect is credible only if the assumption behind the comparison holds in the application.

**Check:** Whether the paper names and defends the identifying assumption underlying its estimator (parallel trends, the factor / low-rank structure with strict exogeneity, or invariance of the shock/relationship under the intervention).

- **Pass:** The paper explicitly identifies the assumption its counterfactual requires and gives at least one argument or piece of evidence for its plausibility in the application.
- **Flag:** The paper presents an effect estimate without ever stating the identifying assumption its estimator depends on, or asserts the assumption with no supporting argument.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Victor Chernozhukov, Kaspar Wüthrich, & Yinchu Zhu. (2021). An Exact and Robust Conformal Inference Method for Counterfactual and Synthetic Controls. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 116(536), 1849-1864. https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.2021.1920957 — p. 1852
  - Kathleen T. Li. (2019). Statistical Inference for Average Treatment Effects Estimated by Synthetic Control Methods. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 115(532), 2068-2083. https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.2019.1686986 — p. 2068
  - Yiqing Xu. (2017). Generalized Synthetic Control Method: Causal Inference with Interactive Fixed Effects Models. Political Analysis, 25(1), 57-76. https://doi.org/10.1017/pan.2016.2 — p. 61

## EST

*Estimation — whether the estimator recovers the target parameter.*

### SYNTH-EST-01 — A synthetic-control paper must report the donor units and the weights assigned to them.

**Scope:** `synthetic_control` · **Severity if flagged:** MEDIUM · **Consensus:** HIGH (6 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** The paper should list the comparison units that make up the synthetic control (a weighted blend of untreated units) and the weight each one receives.

**Why it matters:** Showing which units contribute, and how much, lets readers see that the comparison is a transparent blend of identifiable units that does not extrapolate.

**Check:** Whether the paper lists the control units that receive positive weight in the synthetic control and their weight magnitudes.

- **Pass:** The paper reports the donor units and their assigned weights (e.g., a weights table or a list of the units receiving positive weight and their shares).
- **Flag:** The paper builds a synthetic control but never discloses which donor units enter it or with what weights.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Alberto Abadie, Alexis Diamond, & Jens Hainmueller. (2010). Synthetic Control Methods for Comparative Case Studies: Estimating the Effect of California’s Tobacco Control Program. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 105(490), 493-505. https://doi.org/10.1198/jasa.2009.ap08746 — pp. 494, 500
  - Alberto Abadie & Jérémy L’Hour. (2021). A Penalized Synthetic Control Estimator for Disaggregated Data. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 116(536), 1817-1834. https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.2021.1971535 — p. 1817

## INFER

*Inference — standard errors, tests, and their validity.*

### SYNTH-INFER-01 — A paper reporting a constructed-counterfactual effect must base its uncertainty on a procedure appropriate to few treated units and serially dependent outcomes, not on conventional large-sample independent-observation standard errors alone.

**Scope:** `all` · **Severity if flagged:** HIGH · **Consensus:** HIGH (9 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** The paper should measure uncertainty with a method suited to few treated units and outcomes correlated over time, such as placebo tests on untreated units or fake dates, permutation p-values, resampling that keeps time patterns, or, with several treated units, standard errors grouped by unit.

**Why it matters:** Conventional standard errors that treat observations as independent understate the uncertainty in this setting.

**Check:** Which procedure the paper uses to attach uncertainty or statistical significance to the estimated treated-vs-counterfactual effect.

- **Pass:** The paper reports uncertainty through at least one procedure from this list: a placebo/permutation exercise applying the method to donor units, an in-time (pre-dated) placebo, a permutation or conformal p-value, a block or sieve bootstrap or subsampling scheme that preserves within-unit serial correlation, or -- for a design with several treated units and multiple periods -- standard errors clustered by unit.
- **Flag:** The paper's only stated basis for significance is conventional independent-observation or heteroskedasticity-only (Eicker-Huber-White) standard errors that presume a large-sample normal approximation, or it reports an effect with no uncertainty procedure at all.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Alberto Abadie, Alexis Diamond, & Jens Hainmueller. (2010). Synthetic Control Methods for Comparative Case Studies: Estimating the Effect of California’s Tobacco Control Program. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 105(490), 493-505. https://doi.org/10.1198/jasa.2009.ap08746 — p. 497
  - Alberto Abadie, Alexis Diamond, & Jens Hainmueller. (2011). <b>Synth</b>: An<i>R</i>Package for Synthetic Control Methods in Comparative Case Studies. Journal of Statistical Software, 42(13). https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v042.i13 — p. 5 *(PDF pagination)*
  - Kay H. Brodersen, Fabian Gallusser, Jim Koehler, Nicolas Rémy, & Steven L. Scott. (2015). Inferring causal impact using Bayesian structural time-series models. The Annals of Applied Statistics, 9(1). https://doi.org/10.1214/14-aoas788 — p. 5 *(PDF pagination)*

## REPORT

*Reporting — what the paper must state for a reader to evaluate it.*

### SYNTH-REPORT-01 — A synthetic-control paper should report how the predictor-importance weighting (V) was determined.

**Scope:** `synthetic_control` · **Severity if flagged:** MEDIUM · **Consensus:** HIGH (5 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** The paper should explain how it set the relative importance of each predictor (the V weights) in building the synthetic control, for example by minimizing pre-intervention prediction error, cross-validation, or a justified custom choice.

**Why it matters:** An ad hoc choice can force matching on characteristics that should not be matched and change which units form the comparison.

**Check:** Whether the paper states how the predictor-importance weighting was set -- a data-driven procedure minimizing pre-intervention prediction error, a training/validation split, or a stated custom choice -- as opposed to leaving it unspecified or defaulting silently to an identity-style weighting.

- **Pass:** The paper reports how the predictor-importance weights were chosen (data-driven minimization of pre-period prediction error, cross-validation, or an explicitly justified custom weighting).
- **Flag:** The paper uses covariate predictors to build the synthetic control but never states how their relative importance was weighted.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Alberto Abadie, Alexis Diamond, & Jens Hainmueller. (2011). <b>Synth</b>: An<i>R</i>Package for Synthetic Control Methods in Comparative Case Studies. Journal of Statistical Software, 42(13). https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v042.i13 — p. 4 *(PDF pagination)*
  - Alberto Abadie, Alexis Diamond, & Jens Hainmueller. (2014). Comparative Politics and the Synthetic Control Method. American Journal of Political Science, 59(2), 495-510. https://doi.org/10.1111/ajps.12116 — p. 498
  - Irene Botosaru & Bruno Ferman. (2019). On the role of covariates in the synthetic control method. Econometrics Journal, 22(2), 117-130. https://doi.org/10.1093/ectj/utz001 — p. 126

## DATA

*Data — sample construction and measurement.*

### SYNTH-DATA-01 — The paper must not build its counterfactual from any predictor or control series that is measured post-intervention or is itself affected by the treatment.

**Scope:** `all` · **Severity if flagged:** HIGH · **Consensus:** HIGH (3 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** The paper should build its comparison only from predictors and control series measured before the intervention or argued to be unaffected by it.

**Why it matters:** A variable that the intervention itself moves biases the estimated effect.

**Check:** Whether any variable used to construct the counterfactual (a matching predictor or a control / covariate series) is measured after the intervention or is itself plausibly moved by the treatment.

- **Pass:** Every matching predictor and control series used to build the counterfactual is measured before the intervention or is explicitly argued to be unaffected by it.
- **Flag:** The paper builds the counterfactual using a predictor or control series that is measured after the intervention or is visibly affected by the treatment.
- **When silent:** PASS

**Further reading**
  - Alberto Abadie, Alexis Diamond, & Jens Hainmueller. (2011). <b>Synth</b>: An<i>R</i>Package for Synthetic Control Methods in Comparative Case Studies. Journal of Statistical Software, 42(13). https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v042.i13 — p. 3 *(PDF pagination)*
  - Alberto Abadie, Alexis Diamond, & Jens Hainmueller. (2014). Comparative Politics and the Synthetic Control Method. American Journal of Political Science, 59(2), 495-510. https://doi.org/10.1111/ajps.12116 — p. 498
  - Kay H. Brodersen, Fabian Gallusser, Jim Koehler, Nicolas Rémy, & Steven L. Scott. (2015). Inferring causal impact using Bayesian structural time-series models. The Annals of Applied Statistics, 9(1). https://doi.org/10.1214/14-aoas788 — p. 22 *(PDF pagination)*

### SYNTH-DATA-02 — A paper must report the number of pre- and post-intervention periods underlying its estimate.

**Scope:** `all` · **Severity if flagged:** MEDIUM · **Consensus:** HIGH (6 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** The paper should report how many time periods come before and after the intervention, as counts or as a dated span at the data's frequency.

**Why it matters:** Readers need this to judge whether the method was used where it is credible: a long pre-intervention span reduces bias, and enough later periods are needed to capture the effect.

**Check:** Whether the paper states how many pre-intervention and post-intervention periods (or the date span at its sampling frequency) enter the analysis.

- **Pass:** The paper reports the length of both the pre-intervention and post-intervention windows (period counts or an equivalent dated span at the analysis frequency).
- **Flag:** The reader cannot determine from the paper how many pre-intervention or post-intervention periods the estimate is based on.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Alberto Abadie, Alexis Diamond, & Jens Hainmueller. (2014). Comparative Politics and the Synthetic Control Method. American Journal of Political Science, 59(2), 495-510. https://doi.org/10.1111/ajps.12116 — pp. 497, 500
  - Alberto Abadie, Alexis Diamond, & Jens Hainmueller. (2010). Synthetic Control Methods for Comparative Case Studies: Estimating the Effect of California’s Tobacco Control Program. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 105(490), 493-505. https://doi.org/10.1198/jasa.2009.ap08746 — p. 504
